newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says it won't turn back Albanian refugees.
newsitem.headline: Italy says it won't turn back Albanian refugees.

text.p: Italy said on Saturday it would grant temporary shelter to Albanians fleeing chaos in their homeland as more refugees crossed the Adriatic in a ramshackle flotilla of creaking boats.
But a government official, Nicola Sinisi, said the refugees would not be considered for political asylum because the crisis in Albania was a "degeneration of public order" and not war.
They would be repatriated once Albania's armed anarchy had subsided.

"At this stage we have the duty for humanitarian reasons to keep people who are not able to live in their country. However, we have the duty to do this only for a limited period of time," Sinisi told reporters in the southeast port of Brindisi.

"At the end of this period, they will be repatriated. First on a voluntary basis and later through other means," Sinisi, a junior interior minister, said. He estimated that the period of temporary sanctuary could last about three months.

Sinisi spoke after a crisis meeting of Italian security and immigration chiefs in Brindisi called in response to a developing influx of Albanians in an armada of rusting vessels, many of them decades-old navy patrol boats.

He said the boats had brought 1,600 Albanians to southeast Italy since insurrection began spreading through the impoverished Balkan state this month. They would be impounded so they could not be used for further crossings, he said.
Four more boats arrived in Brindisi shortly after midday (1100 GMT), including one fishing boat with around 190 on board and another with about 75 people.

Italian coastguards said an Albanian navy ship had also been intercepted in the Adriatic and was being escorted to the port. Initial estimates said 200 to 300 people, many of them children, were on board.
The problem of what to do with the refugees has become a pressing issue for Italy, already a magnet for Albanian illegal immigrants.
Their arrival has raised fears in Italy of a repeat of the tide of 40,000 Albanians who flooded into southeast ports in 1991 after Stalinist rule crumbled in Europe's poorest state.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said in Naples earlier on Saturday that Italy should brace for a huge influx.
"We are facing a massive phenomenon because unfortunately this week the Albanian state has fallen apart," Napolitano said.

But Sinisi said the impounding of boats already in Italy and a reported scarcity of seagoing vessels still off Albania would contain the problem. "There is no crisis situation...we don't envisage a mass exodus," he told reporters.

He said many of the Albanians who had arrived had been fingerprinted. About 150 of them were deserting servicemen and a number of prisoners who escaped jails stormed by rioters in Albania. The ex-inmates were being watched closely, he said.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) on Friday urged Italy and Greece to allow Albanians fleeing the turmoil, sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid savings schemes, to enter and stay "as long as necessary".
Napolitano said Italy, and particularly the southeast Puglia region, was accommodating the Albanians at various sites that had been earmarked for such an eventuality.

The chief of police in the Adriatic port of Ancona said the Interior Ministry had advised police in coastal cities to prepare for the eventual arrival of Albanians from parts of the country such as Puglia that no longer had space.
A pregnant women who arrived in the southernmost port of Otranto on Friday with her husband and two children, gave birth to a boy on Saturday in a nearby hospital.
